chapters.title: Ordinary differential equations
chapters.what: An ODE gives the rate of change of a state as a function of the state: x′ = f(t, x). Its solution is a curve that follows the arrows of the slope (or phase) field from an initial condition.
chapters.looks: 2D: the slope field (one equation) or the phase plane (two). 3D: the whole family of solutions as a surface, a trajectory rising in time, or a strange attractor.
chapters.change: Swap Runge–Kutta for Euler and enlarge h: the error grows and a conserved energy starts to drift.
chapters.use: Radioactive decay, populations and epidemics, circuits, oscillators, weather.
misc: A numerical solution is not the solution — check it against a smaller h.

chapters.title: Laplace transforms and transfer functions
chapters.what: The Laplace transform turns a linear ODE into algebra: G(s) = output/input. The poles of G (where it is infinite) decide everything: decay rates, oscillation frequencies, stability.
chapters.looks: 2D: the time response to a step, impulse or sine. 3D: log|G(s)| over the complex s-plane — poles are spikes, and the amber cut along the imaginary axis is the frequency response.
chapters.change: Close the loop and raise the gain K: the poles move and the overshoot grows.
chapters.use: Control systems, circuits, suspensions, servo motors, vibration isolation.
misc: A pole in the right half-plane means instability, however small.
The frequency response is G on the imaginary axis, not on the real axis.

chapters.title: Partial differential equations
chapters.what: A PDE links rates in time and space. Heat diffuses (u_t = α u_xx), waves travel (u_tt = c² u_xx), steady fields satisfy Laplace's equation; boundary and initial conditions pick the solution.
chapters.looks: 2D: the profile u(x) at the current time over the initial one (dashed). 3D: the whole space–time surface u(x, t), or the steady temperature of a plate.
chapters.change: Raise r = αΔt/Δx² above ½ (or the Courant number above 1) and the explicit scheme blows up.
chapters.use: Heat treatment, string instruments, groundwater, electrostatics, weather and climate models.
misc: A stable scheme is not automatically accurate.
Laplace's equation has no time: the plate shown is where diffusion ends up.

examples.title: Heat in a rod: sin(πx) decays as e^{−απ²t}
examples.world: A rod with both ends in ice water; the finite-difference result tracks Fourier's exact solution.

examples.title: Too large a time step: FTCS blows up
examples.world: Explicit schemes need r ≤ ½; Crank–Nicolson (1947) is stable for any step.

examples.title: The steady temperature of a plate heated along one edge

chapters.title: Fourier analysis
chapters.what: Any reasonable periodic signal is a sum of sines and cosines; the discrete Fourier transform finds those frequencies in sampled data.
chapters.looks: 2D: the magnitude spectrum — one spike per tone. 3D: a spectrogram, the spectrum sliding along in time, or the sine components stacked.
chapters.change: Raise a tone above half the sampling rate and it reappears at the wrong frequency (aliasing); shift it off a bin and the spike leaks unless windowed.
chapters.use: Audio and music, vibration monitoring, radar and sonar chirps, image compression.
misc: The DFT only knows frequencies up to fs/2.
More samples improve resolution (fs/N), not the maximum frequency.

examples.title: Building a square wave from odd harmonics
examples.world: Digital clocks and PWM power electronics are square waves.

examples.title: A triangle wave converges fast (1/k²)
